Identity.History: A tropaeum (Greek tropaion) was a battlefield victory monument erected at the point where the defeated enemy had turned and fled. It was typically made by fastening captured armor, shields, helmets, and weapons to a wooden post or tree trunk and dedicating the display to a god, most often Zeus. For Thebes, such trophies were closely associated with its dramatic victories over Sparta: after Leuctra in 371 BC, where Epaminondas shattered the Spartan army, the Thebans erected a trophy commemorating the rout, and similar monuments followed other Boeotian successes during the period of Theban ascendancy. These trophies served not only as religious dedications but also as highly visible statements of military prestige and political dominance.
